subject: Art & Design
title: Color Accessibility: Designing for Everyone
description: A micro-lesson that makes Color Accessibility: Designing for Everyone usable.

hook.text: 8% of men have some form of color blindness. That's 1 in 12 of your male users.

buildup.text: Red-green color blindness is the most common. A red error message on a green form is invisible.

discovery.text: Never rely on color alone to convey meaning. Add icons, labels, or patterns as a second channel.

twist.text: High contrast isn't just for accessibility. It improves readability for everyone in bright sunlight.

climax.text: WCAG guidelines require a 4.5:1 contrast ratio for normal text. Free tools can check this instantly.

punchline.text: Accessible color isn't a constraint. It's better design.

quiz.question: What percentage of men have some form of color blindness?

details.summary: Color accessibility ensures designs work for people with visual impairments, including color blindness, low vision, and screen reader users. WCAG guidelines require minimum contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text) and forbid color as the sole means of conveying information.
details.whyItMatters: Accessible color design isn't just ethical — it's legally required in many jurisdictions and commercially smart. Inaccessible websites face lawsuits, and poor contrast frustrates all users in bright sunlight, on cheap monitors, or with aging eyes.
takeaways: WCAG requires 4.5:1 contrast for normal text readability
Color alone must never be the sole information carrier
Accessibility is legally required and commercially beneficial

faq.question: What does a 4.5:1 contrast ratio mean?
faq.answer: It means the lighter color reflects 4.5 times more light than the darker one. Pure black on white is 21:1 (maximum). Light gray (#767676) on white is approximately 4.5:1 (minimum for normal text). Online contrast checkers like WebAIM's tool calculate this ratio from any two hex values.

faq.question: Does dark mode automatically satisfy accessibility?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Dark mode can improve or worsen accessibility depending on implementation. Very light text on very dark backgrounds can cause halation (glowing effect) for users with astigmatism. The same WCAG contrast ratios apply — test dark mode designs just as rigorously as light mode.
